def: To restore nerve supply to a tissue, such as a muscle regaining function after nerve regeneration.
Regeneration of methionine by adding a methyl group to homocysteine, using methylcobalamin (vitamin B12) and methyltetrahydrofolate. Deficiency of B12 or folate raises homocysteine and traps folate.
A rare kidney tumor of juxtaglomerular cells that secretes renin, causing hypertension with high aldosterone and low potassium, typically in young adults.
Enlargement of one or both kidneys, seen for example in polycystic kidney disease, hydronephrosis or infiltrative disease.

An oral diabetes drug that closes pancreatic beta-cell potassium channels to trigger short-acting insulin release at meals. Like sulfonylureas it can cause hypoglycemia, but it acts at a different binding site.
To return a cell's membrane potential to its negative resting value after depolarization, mainly through potassium efflux.
Re-narrowing of an artery after angioplasty or stenting, caused by neointimal smooth muscle growth. Drug-eluting stents reduce it.
A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clots, used as a thrombolytic in acute myocardial infarction.
The non-infective, feeding larval stage of nematodes such as Strongyloides, with a short esophagus; it molts into the infective filariform larva.
Linear cracks or fissures in the skin, especially radiating from the mouth corners; in congenital syphilis they form scars around the mouth.
Describes shortening of the proximal limb segments (upper arm and thigh), as in achondroplasia.
A modified uridine (5-methyluridine) found in the T-psi-C loop of transfer RNA.

A drug that stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase, raising cGMP and relaxing pulmonary vessels; used for pulmonary arterial hypertension and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Contraindicated in pregnancy and with nitrates or PDE-5 inhibitors.
An oral phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor that raises cAMP and reduces airway inflammation, used to prevent exacerbations in severe COPD.
Toward the nose or head end of the body; in the brain, toward the frontal pole.
A dopamine agonist given as a skin patch for Parkinson disease and restless legs syndrome.
Stacks of red blood cells resembling rolls of coins on a blood smear, caused by high plasma proteins such as in multiple myeloma.
New abnormal blood vessel growth on the iris, driven by ischemia-induced VEGF in conditions like proliferative diabetic retinopathy; can cause neovascular glaucoma.
The pattern of folds (rugae) in a hollow organ lining, such as the stomach, which flatten when the organ distends.
Small outpouchings or pocket-like dilations of a wall, such as the laryngeal saccule or bladder wall pouches.
A ligament running from the sacrum to the ischial spine; with the sacrotuberous ligament it forms the greater and lesser sciatic foramina and anchors the pelvis.
A red basic dye used as the counterstain in Gram staining, coloring gram-negative bacteria pink.
Rapid propagation of action potentials in myelinated axons, where the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier.
Containing or consisting of blood, as in sanguineous fluid or drainage.
Relating to the sarcomere, the contractile unit of striated muscle; sarcomeric protein mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Relating to the scapula and humerus, as in the scapulohumeral rhythm or the glenohumeral muscles connecting them.
Psychotic illness with schizophrenia symptoms lasting 1 to 6 months, diagnosed before the 6-month threshold for schizophrenia.
A genetic condition of multiple schwannomas (nerve sheath tumors) that, unlike neurofibromatosis type 2, spares the vestibular nerves; linked to SMARCB1 and LZTR1 mutations.
Describes hardening with calcium deposition, as in sclerocalcific (senile calcific) aortic stenosis.
Plural of scotoma: areas of partial or complete vision loss within the visual field.
A monoclonal antibody that blocks interleukin-17A, used for plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.
A procedure to create or enlarge a hole in the atrial septum, such as balloon atrial septostomy to improve mixing in transposition of the great arteries.
Drugs such as cholestyramine, colestipol and colesevelam that bind bile acids in the gut to lower LDL cholesterol. They can raise triglycerides and cause bloating.
The point at which antibodies against an infectious agent first become detectable in the blood after infection or vaccination.
Describes a couple in which one partner has an infection such as HIV and the other does not.
Describes fluid or drainage that is a mix of serum and blood, appearing pink or pale red.
Noninflammatory, painless bilateral swelling of the salivary glands, mainly parotids, associated with alcohol use, diabetes, bulimia and malnutrition.
An immature red blood cell with iron-laden mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus (ring sideroblast), seen in sideroblastic anemia.
Having an affinity for iron; describes organisms or tissues that thrive on or take up iron.
Relating to sigmoidoscopy, endoscopic examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
